contract: choose_weights(excess_returns, context) -> array of N finite positions x. excess_returns is a (120, N) float array of the previous 120 monthly excess returns (decimal, oldest first) of the task's N assets; context = {'cost_rate': 0.005, 'window': 120, 'max_gross': 20.0, 'risk_free': (120,) monthly T-bill returns, 'previous_weights': drifted relative weights just before rebalancing (None in the first month)}. The evaluator forms DeMiguel-Garlappi-Uppal relative weights w = x/|sum(x)| (sum(x) must be nonzero and sum|w| <= 20), holds w for the next month, charges 0.5% of sum|w - previous_weights| per rebalance and requires wealth to stay positive. Score: monthly Sharpe ratio of the net out-of-sample excess returns over every month of the task period (maximize); the 1/N rule is recomputed on the same months for comparison
notes: Same rolling-window backtest as the DGU datasets, applied to a dataset DGU did not use; the machinery is checked against DGU's published 1/N values on their datasets only.

Data sources, generated instances, evaluation budgets and protocol differences are specified in the candidate contract, requirements and notes; scores are not automatically comparable with published results.
name: Finance: Out-of-sample portfolio choice against 1/N (49 industries)
description: Choose each month's portfolio of 49 US industry portfolios using only the previous 120 months of returns, a setting where estimation error is severe. The evaluator recomputes the Sharpe ratio of the next-month returns net of 50 bp trading costs over 1979-07 to 2025-09 and compares it with the 1/N rule.
benchmark: Finance: Out-of-sample portfolio choice against 1/N (49 industries)
paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

sources.locator: Sections 2-3: rolling-window protocol, relative weights, Sharpe ratio and 50 bp costs; the 49-industry dataset is not one of DGU's datasets.
49 industry portfolios (value-weighted, complete from 1969-07) and the Fama/French T-bill series, monthly; CRSP 202509 files pinned in catalog/finance-data-lock.json.

limitations: DGU did not study this 49-industry dataset; the protocol is theirs but no published number is reproduced for it, and with N = 49 and a 120-month window the sample covariance matrix is poorly conditioned.

The evaluation months are public and fixed. Strategies or hyperparameters tuned on them overfit, and a candidate that reads the prepared files or embeds remembered returns could look ahead; the evaluator only prevents look-ahead through its interface. Treat scores as development scores and freeze a candidate before testing it on months after 2025-09.

A monthly Sharpe ratio estimated from 50 to 52 years of returns has a standard error of about 0.04, so differences from 1/N below that size are not statistically meaningful; the one-sided Jobson-Korkie-Memmel p-value against 1/N is reported in the details.

Returns are value-weighted CRSP portfolio returns from the CRSP 202509 vintage of the French library; later vintages revise history slightly. Costs are a flat 50 bp of traded value with no market impact, borrowing spread, short-sale fees or taxes, and positions are financed at the one-month T-bill rate.

Deviations from DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal: the scored period extends to 2025-09, returns are net of costs (their Sharpe table is gross), the first allocation is free, gross exposure is capped at 20 and a strategy whose wealth reaches zero is invalid.

sources.title: Optimal Versus Naive Diversification: How Inefficient is the 1/N Portfolio Strategy?

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Choose portfolio weights that perform well out of sample when expected returns and covariances must be estimated from short return histories.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Estimation error can make optimized portfolios worse than naive diversification; DGU find that none of 14 optimizing models reliably beats 1/N, so robust portfolio choice remains a central problem for investors and for asset-pricing research.

papers.title: Optimal Versus Naive Diversification: How Inefficient is the 1/N Portfolio Strategy?
papers.primary_goal: Determine whether portfolio rules derived from mean-variance optimization, including rules designed to reduce estimation error, outperform naive 1/N diversification out of sample.
papers.task_relation: The local task applies DGU's rolling-window protocol to 49 industry portfolios, a larger cross-section that DGU did not use, and scores net-of-cost Sharpe ratios.

science_relevance.reason: The cited paper's main objective is the out-of-sample performance of portfolio rules relative to 1/N, which is exactly what the task scores.
